CWE-179.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Early Validation
CWE-179.question: Does this function validate input and only afterwards apply a step that modifies it, so the value used differs from the value checked?

any: a check for forbidden characters, paths or patterns runs, then the value is URL-decoded, unescaped, normalised, stripped or filtered before use
validation inspects one representation and a later conversion (case folding, Unicode normalisation, path resolution) produces the value that is acted on
all decoding, canonicalising and filtering are done first and the final value is the one validated
the value is not changed between the check and its use
the check is repeated after the final transformation

distinguish_from.CWE-180: the modification after the check is canonicalisation or decoding
distinguish_from.CWE-181: the modification after the check is a filter that removes or replaces content

CWE-180.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize
CWE-180.question: Does this function check input for bad content and only afterwards decode, normalise or resolve it into the form that is actually used?

any: a blacklist or pattern check runs on a path, URL or string, then the value is URL-decoded, HTML-unescaped, Unicode-normalised or case-folded
a path is checked for '..' or a prefix and then passed through realpath, path resolution or symlink following before use
javascript: a check precedes decodeURIComponent, path.normalize, path.resolve or String.prototype.normalize on the same value
python: a check precedes urllib.parse.unquote, os.path.normpath, os.path.realpath or unicodedata.normalize on the same value

any: the value is decoded and canonicalised first, and the canonical form is what is checked and used
the value used after the check is the identical, unmodified one that was checked

distinguish_from.CWE-181: the step after validation removes or replaces content rather than canonicalising it

CWE-181.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Filter
CWE-181.question: Does this function validate data and only afterwards run a filter that strips or replaces parts of it, so the filtered result is never re-checked?

any: a check approves the input, then a later replace, strip or sanitiser removes characters or tags, possibly joining fragments into forbidden content
a single-pass removal of a token such as '../' or '<script>' follows the validation step and its output is used directly
filtering happens first and validation runs on the filtered result
the filter is applied repeatedly until no change, then validated
nothing alters the data between the check and its use

distinguish_from.CWE-180: the step after validation is decoding or canonicalisation rather than removing content

CWE-248.name: Uncaught Exception
CWE-248.question: Can a C++ exception escape this function where nothing will catch it, such as from a destructor, a noexcept function, main or a thread entry point?

cpp: a destructor, move operation or noexcept function contains throw or calls code that can throw (new, at(), stoi, container growth) without a try/catch
main, a std::thread entry function or a C callback invokes throwing code with no catch around it
a throw statement whose exception type is not caught anywhere visible in the function and the function is a top-level entry
the throwing calls are wrapped in try with a catch that handles or logs the exception
the function is an ordinary member or free function that lets the exception propagate to callers able to catch it

distinguish_from.CWE-396: an exception is caught, but with an overly general catch clause

CWE-396.name: Declaration of Catch for Generic Exception
CWE-396.question: Does this function catch an overly general exception type, so unrelated failures are handled by the same code?

cpp: catch (...) or catch (const std::exception&) around code that can fail in several distinct ways, without re-throwing
python: a bare except:, except Exception: or except BaseException: that handles the error without re-raising

any: the catch names the specific exception types the code can raise
the broad handler only logs and then re-throws or re-raises the exception
the broad handler is at a top-level boundary (main loop, request handler, thread entry) whose job is to stop the process crashing

distinguish_from.CWE-397: the function throws or declares a generic exception rather than catching one
distinguish_from.CWE-248: no catch exists and the exception escapes

CWE-397.name: Declaration of Throws for Generic Exception
CWE-397.question: Does this function throw or raise a generic, base exception type instead of a specific one that callers could handle?

cpp: throw std::exception(), throw std::runtime_error for unrelated failure kinds, or throw of a plain int or string literal
a dynamic exception specification or documentation comment declaring only a base type
python: raise Exception(...) or raise BaseException(...) rather than a specific subclass

any: thrown or raised exceptions are specific types such as ValueError, KeyError, std::invalid_argument or a project-defined subclass
the function only re-throws a caught exception unchanged

distinguish_from.CWE-396: the function catches a generic exception rather than throwing one

CWE-408.name: Incorrect Behavior Order: Early Amplification
CWE-408.question: Does this function do costly work (heavy computation, large allocation, decompression, database or network calls) for a request before checking who is asking and whether they may?

any: the body parses, decompresses, hashes, queries or allocates large buffers from the request before the authentication or permission check runs
an expensive call such as key derivation, image processing or report generation precedes the session or token check
authentication and authorisation are checked first, and failure returns before any costly step
the function is reached only after middleware or a decorator that authenticates (visible as an attribute or wrapper on the function)
the work done before the check is cheap and bounded, such as reading a header

distinguish_from.CWE-799: there is no limit on how often the caller may repeat the request at all

CWE-430.name: Deployment of Wrong Handler
CWE-430.question: Does this function route an object, file or request to a handler chosen from an unreliable or contradictory signal, so the wrong code processes it?

any: the handler, parser or renderer is picked from a file extension, sniffed content or client-supplied type that can disagree with the declared or verified type
a dispatch table or lookup falls back to a generic or raw handler (for example serving a script as plain source) when the expected one is not matched
an explicit type field is ignored in favour of guessing the type from the content
the handler is selected from a fixed allow-list keyed on a verified type, and unknown types are rejected
the declared type and the detected type are compared and a mismatch is refused
there is only one handler and no dispatch decision is made

distinguish_from.CWE-431: no handler exists at all for the event or type, rather than the wrong one being chosen
distinguish_from.CWE-434: the issue is accepting an uploaded file of a dangerous type rather than which handler processes it

CWE-431.name: Missing Handler
CWE-431.question: Does this function leave an expected event, error, case or exception with no handler, so it goes unprocessed or is passed up unhandled?

any: a switch or match over an enum, message type or state has no default and omits values that can occur
an event, signal or callback registration expects a handler but none is supplied for a case the code can raise
c: a call whose failure must be handled (an error code, a signal) has no branch dealing with the failure case
cpp: a std::future from std::async is discarded or never get() is called, so a stored exception is never observed
javascript: a promise chain or async call has no catch and is not awaited inside a try, or an emitter's 'error' event has no listener
python: a thread, task or callback can raise but nothing catches or reports the exception
rust: a match uses a catch-all arm that silently does nothing for variants that need handling

any: every possible case, event or error has an explicit branch, or a default branch that handles or reports it
the function deliberately lets the error propagate to its caller as part of its documented contract
rust: the match is exhaustive and the compiler forces every variant to be handled

distinguish_from.CWE-430: a handler exists but the code dispatches to the wrong one
distinguish_from.CWE-248: a C++ exception escapes a function boundary where nothing can catch it

CWE-455.name: Non-exit on Failed Initialization
CWE-455.question: Does this initialisation function carry on, perhaps with insecure defaults, after a security-relevant setup step fails?

any: loading a configuration, key, certificate, policy or crypto module fails and the code logs or ignores it, then continues with defaults or a disabled check
an initialisation error sets a flag or returns success anyway, so the program runs without the protection it set up
c: the return value of an init call such as SSL_CTX_use_certificate_file or a crypto library init is ignored or only printed
cpp: a constructor or init method catches the exception from loading a key, certificate or config and carries on with defaults

any: a failed security setup step aborts start-up, returns an error to the caller or throws
the fallback taken on failure is the more restrictive behaviour (deny all, refuse connections)
the failing step is not security-relevant, such as an optional cosmetic setting

distinguish_from.CWE-431: the failure has no handling path at all rather than a path that continues

CWE-480.name: Use of Incorrect Operator
CWE-480.question: Does this function use the wrong operator in an expression, so a test or calculation means something different from what was intended?

any: & or | used where && or || was clearly meant (or the reverse), changing evaluation or result
a comparison operator that is reversed or off by one, such as < for <=, in a security or bounds check
c: = used inside an if or while condition where == was meant, or == used as a statement where = was meant
javascript: == used where strict === was needed so coercion lets unexpected values pass
python: 'is' used to compare strings or numbers where == was meant, or 'and'/'or' mixed up with & and |
rust: a bitwise & or | on bools where short-circuit && or || was needed to avoid evaluating the right side

any: the operator matches the evident intent and the surrounding code agrees
the unusual operator is deliberate and explained, such as bit flags tested with & or an assignment in a condition wrapped in extra parentheses and compared

distinguish_from.CWE-481: the specific mistake is = where == was meant
distinguish_from.CWE-482: the specific mistake is == where = was meant
distinguish_from.CWE-783: the operators are right but precedence groups them wrongly

CWE-481.name: Assigning instead of Comparing
CWE-481.question: Does this function use an assignment (=) in a condition where a comparison (==) was evidently intended?

c: if (x = value) or while (x = value) where the variable is not otherwise used as the result of a call and the right side is a constant or another variable
an assignment inside a compound condition such as a && (b = c) that reads like an equality test
the assignment captures a call result and is explicitly compared, such as if ((p = malloc(n)) != NULL) or while ((c = getc(f)) != EOF)
the condition uses == or another comparison operator
the idiom is clearly intentional, wrapped in double parentheses to capture a value that is then used
cpp: a C++17 if (auto p = lookup()) or if (auto x = f(); x == y) declaration, which deliberately tests the new variable

distinguish_from.REL-111: the assignment's value is deliberately used as an operand and the concern is style or clarity, not a mistaken comparison
distinguish_from.CWE-482: the mistake is the reverse, a comparison where an assignment was meant

CWE-482.name: Comparing instead of Assigning
CWE-482.question: Does this function contain a comparison (==) used as a stand-alone statement where an assignment was evidently intended?

c: an expression statement such as x == 0; whose result is discarded
a for-loop init or increment clause written with == instead of =, so the variable is never set
the result of every comparison is used in a condition, return or assignment
the variable is assigned with = before use and the == appears only inside tests

distinguish_from.CWE-481: the mistake is an assignment where a comparison was meant

CWE-483.name: Incorrect Block Delimitation
CWE-483.question: Does this function have an if, else, loop or similar body without braces whose indentation shows several statements were meant to be controlled?

c: two or more indented lines follow an if, else, for or while with no braces, so only the first is conditional
a semicolon directly after if (...) or while (...) makes the intended body run unconditionally
a macro expanding to several statements is used as the unbraced body of an if
every multi-statement body is wrapped in braces
an unbraced body is a single statement and the following line is visibly not indented as part of it
multi-statement macros are wrapped in do { ... } while (0)

distinguish_from.REL-123: the body is a single unbraced statement and there is no sign that more were intended

CWE-584.name: Return Inside Finally Block
CWE-584.question: Does this function return (or break or continue) from inside a finally block, discarding an exception or result from the try block?

any: a return, break or continue statement inside a finally clause
c: a return or goto leaving a Microsoft __finally block
javascript: return inside finally in a try/catch/finally, which overrides any thrown error or earlier return
python: return, break or continue inside finally:, which silences an in-flight exception

any: the finally block only releases resources and has no return, break or continue
the return is in the try or except/catch block, not in finally
c: standard C and C++ have no finally clause; RAII destructors and cleanup labels cannot discard an exception this way
rust: Rust has no finally clause; Drop and explicit cleanup cannot swallow a panic this way

distinguish_from.CWE-396: an exception is swallowed by a broad catch clause rather than by finally

CWE-617.name: Reachable Assertion
CWE-617.detached: assertions are common in C, while its MITRE parent CWE-705 (control flow scoping) rarely applies
CWE-617.question: Does this function contain an assertion that input from outside the program could make fail, ending the process or request?

any: an assert or abort-on-failure check tests a value that comes from a parameter fed by external input, a file, a network message or user data, and that value is not validated before the assertion
c: assert() or a project assertion macro checks a length, count, index or state read from input
python: assert checks request, file or message content (note that python -O removes these, which is a separate concern)
rust: assert!, panic!, unreachable!, unwrap() or expect() fires on a malformed input value rather than a programming error

any: the assertion checks an internal invariant that only a programming error could violate, such as a pointer the function itself just set
the asserted value has already been validated on every path, with an error returned for bad input
the assertion only exists in debug builds and the same condition is handled at run time
c: static_assert or _Static_assert, which is checked at compile time

distinguish_from.REL-026: the hazard is an unguarded division, dereference or index rather than an assertion

CWE-670.name: Always-Incorrect Control Flow Implementation
CWE-670.question: Does this function contain a control-flow path that can never do what the surrounding code plainly intends, whatever the input?

any: a condition that is always true or always false because of a wrong operator, a stray semicolon or a typo, so a branch always or never runs
a loop, return or break placed so that the intended statements are skipped or repeated on every pass
a case falls through, or an else binds to the wrong if, so the wrong block runs every time
the branching and loop structure matches the evident intent on every path
a constant condition is deliberate, such as while (true) with a clear break or a feature flag
the defect only appears for particular input values, which is a different class of logic error

distinguish_from.CWE-480: the root cause is a specific wrong operator such as = for ==
distinguish_from.CWE-483: the root cause is a missing pair of braces around a multi-statement body
distinguish_from.CWE-783: the root cause is operator precedence grouping an expression differently from the intent

CWE-674.name: Uncontrolled Recursion
CWE-674.question: Does this function recurse, directly or through callbacks, to a depth controlled by input or data with no depth limit?

any: a function calls itself on nested input (JSON, XML, trees, expressions, directories) without a depth counter or maximum
mutual recursion through helper functions or visitor callbacks driven by data structure depth
a recursive call whose base case may never be reached for some inputs, such as cycles in a graph without a visited set
a depth parameter is checked against a fixed maximum before each recursive call
the recursion depth is bounded by a small constant or by the logarithm of the size, as in balanced divide and conquer
the algorithm uses an explicit stack or queue instead of recursion

distinguish_from.CWE-776: the unbounded recursion is XML entity expansion through a DTD
distinguish_from.REL-133: C or C++ code simply contains recursion, regardless of whether the depth is input-controlled
distinguish_from.CWE-835: an iterative loop, not recursion, never terminates

CWE-691.name: Insufficient Control Flow Management
CWE-691.question: Does the function have control flow that could go wrong: loops, error handling, ordering of steps, short-circuit logic, state machines or workflow checks?

any: loops whose exit depends on input or on values updated in the body, or recursion
exception handlers, error returns, signal handlers, goto or early returns that skip later steps
a sequence of steps whose order matters, such as validate then use, or a multi-step workflow or state machine
conditions with &&, || or side effects, or retries and repeated actions without limits
the function is a straight-line accessor, constructor or simple wrapper with no loops, branches on input or error handling
the function only declares data or returns a constant

CWE-696.name: Incorrect Behavior Order
CWE-696.question: Does this function perform related steps, such as checking, transforming, authorising or releasing, in an order that defeats their purpose?

any: input is validated and then changed (decoded, normalised, trimmed, filtered) before it is used
an expensive or state-changing operation runs before the authentication or permission check
a resource is used after the step that should have prepared it, or released before its last use in the same sequence
privileges are dropped after, rather than before, untrusted work begins
every transformation happens before the check, and the checked value is exactly what is used
authorisation and validation precede any costly or side-effecting action on all paths
the steps are independent, so their order does not matter

distinguish_from.CWE-179: the order problem is specifically validating input before it is modified
distinguish_from.CWE-408: the order problem is specifically doing costly work before authenticating the caller

CWE-698.name: Execution After Redirect (EAR)
CWE-698.question: Does this function send a redirect response and then keep executing code that should have been skipped?

any: a redirect (Location header, 302) is issued in an access check or error branch with no return, exit or throw after it, so sensitive work below still runs
c: a CGI or web handler prints a Location header and then continues to the protected code
javascript: res.redirect() or reply.redirect() inside an if, without a return, followed by further processing or res.send
python: redirect() or HttpResponseRedirect created in a branch but not returned, so the view continues

any: the redirect is immediately followed by return, exit, die or a thrown exception on every path
the redirect is the last statement of the function
python: the redirect object is returned, or abort/raise is used, which stops the view

distinguish_from.CWE-705: control flow continues wrongly after something other than a redirect

CWE-705.name: Incorrect Control Flow Scoping
CWE-705.question: Does this function transfer control to the wrong place after finishing a task or detecting an error, such as continuing, swallowing an exception or jumping out without cleanup?

any: after an error or redirect is detected the function carries on with normal processing instead of returning
an exception is caught too broadly or swallowed, or a finally block overrides it with a return
control leaves the function abnormally (longjmp, exit, abort, process termination) without releasing what it holds
every error path returns, throws or jumps to a cleanup label and stops normal processing
exceptions are caught narrowly and either handled or re-thrown

distinguish_from.CWE-698: processing continues after a redirect response is sent
distinguish_from.CWE-584: a return inside a finally block discards an exception
distinguish_from.CWE-396: the problem is catching an overly general exception type

CWE-768.name: Incorrect Short Circuit Evaluation
CWE-768.question: Does this function put an operation with side effects in a later operand of && or ||, so it is skipped whenever the earlier operand decides the result?

any: a call that changes state, frees, logs, increments or assigns appears to the right of && or || in a condition
code after the condition assumes the right-hand side ran, such as using a variable it assigns
python: a state-changing call placed after 'and' or 'or' in a condition

any: every operand after the first is a pure test with no side effects
the skipping is the intent, such as p != NULL && p->x or a guarded lazy initialisation
the side effect is performed in a separate statement before the condition

distinguish_from.REL-112: the C or C++ code places a state-changing operation on the right of && or ||, the narrower rule for those languages

CWE-776.name: Improper Restriction of Recursive Entity References in DTDs ('XML Entity Expansion')
CWE-776.question: Does this function parse XML with DTD processing and entity expansion enabled, without limits on entity expansion?

any: untrusted XML is parsed with a parser configured to load DTDs or expand internal entities
c: libxml2 called with XML_PARSE_NOENT or XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD on untrusted data, or with XML_PARSE_HUGE
javascript: libxmljs parseXml called with noent: true, or another parser with entity expansion switched on
python: xml.dom.minidom, xml.sax or lxml.etree used on untrusted input with resolve_entities enabled or without defusedxml
rust: an XML crate configured to expand custom DTD entities on untrusted input

any: DTDs are disabled or rejected, or entity expansion is turned off
the parser enforces an entity expansion limit, or the XML comes only from a trusted constant
python: defusedxml is used, or lxml with resolve_entities=False

distinguish_from.CWE-674: recursion depth is uncontrolled in the program's own code rather than in XML entity expansion

CWE-783.name: Operator Precedence Logic Error
CWE-783.question: Does this function contain an expression whose operator precedence groups it differently from what the code evidently intends?

any: a bitwise test such as x & MASK == 0, where == binds before &
an assignment of a call result mixed with a comparison without parentheses, such as if (rc = f() != 0)
shift or arithmetic mixed without parentheses where the intended grouping differs, such as a << 1 + b
c: *p++ or *p.x used where (*p)++ or (*p).x was intended
cpp: std::cout << x & mask or std::cout << ok ? a : b, where << binds before & and ?: so the stream, not the value, is tested
javascript: a ternary or ?? combined with + or || without parentheses, such as 'a' + x ? y : z
python: not a == b or a & b == c where the grouping differs from intent
rust: a cast or unary minus combined with method calls or bit operators where the grouping is not what is wanted

any: parentheses make the intended grouping explicit
the expression uses only operators whose standard precedence gives the obvious reading, such as a * b + c

distinguish_from.REL-104: the grouping is correct but the mixed operators lack clarifying parentheses
distinguish_from.CWE-480: the wrong operator is used, not the right ones grouped wrongly

CWE-799.name: Improper Control of Interaction Frequency
CWE-799.question: Does this function let a caller repeat an action (login attempt, request, message, code check) without any limit on how often or how many times?

any: a login, password reset, OTP or token verification handler with no attempt counter, lockout, delay or rate-limit call
a request handler that sends email or SMS, or performs paid or expensive work, with no throttle per user or address
a loop accepting messages or connections from one peer with no cap
the function consults a rate limiter, attempt counter or lockout before acting
a decorator, middleware or attribute applying a rate limit is visible on the function
the action is harmless to repeat and cheap

distinguish_from.CWE-837: an action meant to happen only once (vote, coupon, signup bonus) can be done more than once
distinguish_from.CWE-408: costly work precedes authentication rather than being unlimited

CWE-834.name: Excessive Iteration
CWE-834.question: Does it contain a loop or recursion whose number of iterations or depth is not clearly bounded?

any: a loop whose bound comes from input, a length field or a count read from data
while (true) or a loop whose exit depends on data, state changes or external events that may never occur
a function that calls itself directly or through a callback, or parses nested structures recursively
an event-loop callback or async handler that blocks in a loop
the function has no loops and no recursion
every loop iterates over a fixed-size collection or a constant range

CWE-835.name: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')
CWE-835.question: Does this function contain a loop whose exit condition can never become true for some reachable state or input?

any: the loop variable is never updated, or is updated in a way that moves away from the exit condition
a loop waits for data or a state change but treats an error, EOF or zero-length result as 'try again' forever
an unsigned counter compared with >= 0, or a narrow counter compared with a wider limit it can never reach
a continue skips the only statement that advances the loop
the loop variable moves monotonically towards a reachable bound on every iteration
an intentional infinite server or event loop with a clear break, return or shutdown signal
the loop has a maximum iteration count or timeout

distinguish_from.CWE-674: the non-terminating construct is recursion, not a loop
distinguish_from.CWE-1322: the loop terminates but blocks a single-threaded event loop while it runs

CWE-837.name: Improper Enforcement of a Single, Unique Action
CWE-837.question: Does this function perform an action that should happen only once per user (vote, redeem, claim, confirm) without checking and recording that it already happened?

any: a coupon, voucher, reward, vote or one-time token is applied without checking a used flag or record
the 'already used' check and the update that marks it used are separate steps without a transaction, lock or unique constraint, so concurrent calls both pass
a one-time token is verified but never invalidated or deleted afterwards
the code atomically checks and marks the action as done (conditional update, unique key, compare-and-set, transaction)
a one-time token is deleted or marked consumed in the same operation that accepts it
repeating the action is harmless and allowed

distinguish_from.CWE-799: the action may be repeated legitimately but there is no limit on frequency

CWE-841.name: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow
CWE-841.question: Does this function perform a step of a multi-step process (checkout, password reset, signup) without confirming the earlier required steps were completed?

any: a handler for a later step acts on a session or order without checking a state or stage field set by the previous step
the step to perform is taken from a client-supplied parameter, allowing steps to be skipped or replayed
a payment, confirmation or reset is completed without verifying the verification step succeeded
the function checks the stored state is exactly the expected predecessor before acting, and rejects otherwise
the process is a single atomic step with no required sequence
a state machine with explicit allowed transitions governs the change

distinguish_from.CWE-696: the function itself performs its internal steps in the wrong order

CWE-1322.name: Use of Blocking Code in Single-threaded, Non-blocking Context
CWE-1322.question: Does this function, running inside a single-threaded event loop or async context, call something that blocks the thread?

any: an async function or event callback performs a busy-wait or long CPU loop on input-sized data
c: a libuv, libevent or epoll callback calls blocking read, write, sleep, connect or DNS lookup on a blocking descriptor
cpp: an Asio, Qt or coroutine handler calls std::this_thread::sleep_for, a blocking future get() or a synchronous socket read
javascript: a request handler or async function uses fs.readFileSync, execSync, child_process sync calls, or a synchronous crypto such as pbkdf2Sync
python: an async def calls time.sleep, requests, blocking socket or file I/O, or subprocess.run instead of awaiting an async equivalent
rust: an async fn calls std::thread::sleep, std::fs, blocking std::net I/O or a blocking mutex lock across an await

any: only non-blocking or awaited async equivalents are used
blocking work is moved to a worker thread or pool, such as run_in_executor, spawn_blocking or a worker thread
the function is not called from an event loop, such as a start-up script or a CLI tool
cpp: the blocking work is posted to a thread pool, for example with asio::post or std::async, and the handler does not wait on it

distinguish_from.CWE-835: the loop never ends at all
